en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Confession (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Acelaka-vagga 42.
The Training Rule on Sending Away.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son said to a bhikkhu who was the co-resident pupil of his brother,
"Come, friend, let us enter the village for alms.
Without having had anything given to him, he sent him away.
“Go, friend; conversation or sitting together with you is not comfortable for me; conversation or sitting alone is comfortable for me.
Then, as the time drew near, that bhikkhu was unable to go for alms, nor could he find anyone to share his meal upon returning;
thus, he went without food. Having gone to the monastery, he reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
Those monks who were of few desires... they complained, grumbled, and spread it about:
"How can the venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta, having said to a monk, ‘Come, friend, let us enter the village for alms,’ dismiss him without having had anything given to him? ...
[and so on] ... "Is it true, Upananda, that you dismissed a monk after saying, ‘Come, friend, let us enter the village for alms,’ without having had anything given to him?"
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, tell a bhikkhu, ‘Come, friend, let us enter the village for alms,’ and then dismiss him without having had anything given to him?”
“Monk, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
‘If a monk says to another monk, “Come, friend, let us enter a village or town for alms,” and then—’”
Whether she has caused it to be given or not, she should dismiss him, saying: “Go, friend; conversation or sitting with you is not comfortable for me;
conversation or sitting alone is comfortable for me. If she does so for this reason alone and no other, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"But whoever" means:
whoever, of whatever kind...
[as before] ...a bhikkhu.
... [as before] ... in this context, "bhikkhu" is intended in this sense. "Bhikkhunī" means another bhikkhu.
"Friend, 'a village or a town' means:
a village, a town, a city, and both a village and a town.
'Having caused it to be given to him'..."
Having caused [someone] to give either gruel, or a meal, or hard food, or soft food.
"Without having caused to give" means without having caused anything at all to be given.
"Should dismiss" means:
desiring to laugh with a woman, desiring to play with her, desiring to sit in private with her, or desiring to engage in improper conduct, he says this:
"Go, friend; conversation or sitting together with you does not give me comfort; [let us be] alone."
If she says, “My conversation or sitting together with you is uncomfortable,” and he dismisses her, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For him who leaves the range of sight or the range of hearing, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Once it has been left, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Making this very condition and no other—
there is no other condition for sending him away—
if he sends him away while he is ordained and perceives him as being ordained, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one sends away one who is fully ordained while being in doubt [of their status], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one sends away one who is fully ordained while perceiving them as not fully ordained, there is an offense of expiation.
If one subjects them to a formal accusation of misconduct (kalīsāsana), there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one incites a person who has not received full ordination, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one brings a message of ill-will, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one perceives a person who has not received full ordination as one who has received full ordination, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one is doubtful that the person is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If the person is not fully ordained and one perceives them as such, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense—
If he sends her away thinking, “We two shall not be able to subsist together”;
or if he sends her away thinking, “Having seen an expensive article, she will give rise to a state of greed”;
or if he sends her away thinking, “Having seen a woman, she will give rise to dissatisfaction.”
If he urges someone, saying, “Bring out rice gruel, or a meal, or fresh food, or solid food for the one who is ill, or for the one staying behind,
or for the guardian of the monastery,” and does not do so because he wishes to engage in improper conduct, but rather urges them because there is a necessary task to be done; this is not an offense.
"In the case of one who is insane,
and in the case of the first offender.
The second training rule on inciting [a nun] is finished.
